items.title: Async Rust, Two Years In: What the Borrow Checker Actually Costs You
items.brief: Two years of stable async Rust have moved the argument from 'is it ready' to what the borrow checker actually asks of working programmers. Cancellation safety is still the one place where the compiler stays silent and the footguns live in documentation instead of types.

items.title: Why I Still Run My Own Email in 2026
items.brief: A thirteen-year personal mail server survives on three habits: plain formats, conservative upgrades, and refusing every managed feature that cannot be exported. The running cost is now under a day of maintenance a year, which the author argues is the true price of owning an address.

items.title: Postgres 18: the Release Notes Are the Feature
items.brief: The Postgres 18 release notes read less like a changelog and more like a statement of direction: asynchronous I/O lands on a default-on path, and the vacuum work finally targets the case every operator actually hits. Each notable change is paired with the benchmark that motivated it.

items.title: A Field Guide to Understanding Any Codebase in a Week
items.brief: Find the data, trace one write path end to end, and only then read the tests. The guide insists a week is enough for any codebase under a million lines, provided you resist fixing things while you read.

items.title: The Boring Technology Behind the Mars Helicopter
items.brief: Ingenuity flew on a Linux box running an unpatched kernel, and the mission succeeded precisely because every component was chosen for flight heritage over capability. The lesson generalizes: exotic parts fail in ways nobody rehearsed.

items.title: The Day the Grid Became a Software Problem
items.brief: Grid operators now dispatch electricity the way cloud operators dispatch compute, and the failure modes have migrated with the software. Three documented near-misses are set out here, and in each one a scheduling bug, not a storm, came closest to dropping load.

items.title: How Tariffs Rewired the Used Server Market
items.brief: Tariff schedules quietly reshaped the secondary server market: rack prices decoupled from hardware age, and whole regions switched from importing refurbished machines to reconditioning domestically. The data comes from five years of public auction results.

items.title: The Ethics of a Default: Notes on Opt-Out Everything
items.brief: Every default is a decision made on behalf of someone who will never open settings. Tracing opt-out design from cookie banners to model-training toggles, the essay asks where consent actually lives when the switch is pre-flipped.

items.title: What a 1987 Bell Labs Memo Predicts About AI Assistants
items.brief: A Bell Labs memo on computer-aided documentation predicts, almost sentence for sentence, how assistants would be used and misused: as a drafting aid, a summary engine, and a way to skip reading. Its proposed safeguards failed for reasons that still apply.

items.title: Reading the Fine Print in Cloud Egress Pricing
items.brief: Egress pricing looks like a line item until a migration makes it a line item you negotiate. The sticker rate matters less than the waiver tiers, and most teams leave free discounts unclaimed because nobody reads past the calculator.

items.title: The Librarian Who Catalogued the Internet's Orphan Pages
items.brief: A one-person project to index pages with no surviving inbound links has catalogued four million documents that would otherwise vanish with their hosts. The hard part is deciding an orphan page is worthless, which requires exactly the judgment no crawler has.

items.title: Latency Is a Design Material
items.brief: Treating latency as an aesthetic constraint rather than a performance metric changes interface design: the pieces users touch get the milliseconds, and the pieces users watch get the wait. Examples from flight booking to text editors show waits made honest rather than hidden.

items.title: A Defense of the Personal Archive
items.brief: Thirty years of personal notes in plain text files survive every platform bankruptcy and every format fashion. The defense is not nostalgia: search over your own writing improves with age, while search over a vendor's improves with their quarter.

items.title: Inside the Archive: How the Wayback Machine Stores a Petabyte a Day
items.brief: The engineering answer to petabyte-a-day ingestion is a stack of boring decisions: append-only storage, aggressive dedupe, and formats chosen to outlive their parsers. A tour of the racks behind the public web's memory.

items.title: A Filesystem in 1,000 Lines of Rust
items.brief: A teaching filesystem that fits in a thousand lines of Rust while keeping crash consistency through a write-ahead journal. Every design cut is paired with the test that would have caught the bug the cut reintroduces.

items.title: Tickless Kernels: What Actually Changed in the Scheduler
items.brief: Removing the periodic timer interrupt was the easy part; the interesting changes are sub-millisecond accounting, timer coalescing, and the debug tooling that quietly assumed a heartbeat. A close look at what the kernel does with all the quiet time.

items.title: Calling Go From Rust: Mapping the Real Costs of the FFI Boundary
items.brief: Go libraries reached from Rust through C-shaped bindings work until garbage collection and goroutine state meet an unsynchronized boundary. The piece maps which calls are safe, which need runtime locks, and why the clean answer is usually a sidecar process.

items.title: Writing an eBPF Verifier Simulation in Rust
items.brief: Reimplementing the eBPF verifier's abstract interpreter in userspace lets tool authors test programs without a kernel nearby. The simulator reproduces the rejection cases that matter and shaves the reboot loop out of the development cycle.

items.title: The Case for Capability-Based Memory in Hobby OSes
items.brief: Capability-based memory protection has been the future since the i4320, but CHERI boards finally make it testable on a desk. The argument: hobby operating systems are where programming models get honest, because nobody there has a compatibility list to protect.

items.title: cgroup v2, Six Years In: Lessons From Shipping It Everywhere
items.brief: Six years of cgroup v2 in production produced a short list of rules: one hierarchy, delegate deliberately, and never let two tools own the same controller. Each rule comes with the incident, not the RFC, that motivated it.

items.title: Porting a Toy Kernel From C to Rust: the Diff, Line by Line
items.brief: A line-by-line port of a teaching kernel from C to Rust, keeping the same linker script and boot path. The diff is boring in the best way: unsafe shrinks to three pages of MMIO, and the borrow checker catches one real double-unmap.

items.title: io_uring Beyond the Benchmarks: Where It Breaks in Production
items.brief: io_uring benchmarks always shine, but production traffic mixes file types and failure modes the benchmarks skip. This inventory of where it breaks — buffered reads on network mounts, registered files going stale — is the checklist the fast path deserves.

items.title: Immutability at the MMU: Page Tables as a Type System
items.brief: Framing MMU page permissions as a type system clarifies what the hardware already proves, what the compiler could prove with annotations, and where the gap that kernel exploits live actually sits. Dense, but the mapping table alone is worth the read.

items.title: Rust in FreeBSD: the First Year of the Gateway
items.brief: The first year of Rust code in the FreeBSD tree produced one driver, a coding standard, and a decision that review capacity, not compiler maturity, is the real constraint. A sober status report from inside a slow-moving tree.

items.title: How Scheduler Bugs Hide: a Tracing Field Guide
items.brief: Scheduler bugs hide because their symptoms are load-shaped: they vanish under tracing and reproduce under customers. This field guide covers the tracing modes that survive production and the signatures that point at priority inversion rather than capacity.

items.title: The Btrfs Decade: What Repair Actually Looks Like
items.brief: Ten years on, Btrfs repair is a known quantity: what scrub catches, what it does not, and why the recommendation flipped from 'avoid' to 'fine with a caveat' on most distributions. The caveat gets its own section.

items.title: Building a Compositor in Rust Without Losing a Frame
items.brief: A Wayland compositor that never misses a frame is less about the language and more about respecting the presentation clock. The write-up covers buffer age, damage tracking, and the one allocation that cost a vblank.

items.title: Userspace Drivers Are Finally Practical — Here's the Catch
items.brief: Drivers in userspace behind small privileged shims are finally practical, thanks to mature VFIO and UIO paths — with real tradeoffs in reset handling and hotplug. The catch, as ever, is DMA: the hardware trusts whoever holds the mappings.

items.title: What Teams Actually Measure When They Measure Agent Productivity
items.brief: Most teams track acceptance rate, which proxies for convenience rather than value. The organizations with useful numbers count reverted changes and rework half-life — and their dashboards look nothing like the vendor slides.

items.title: Disaster-Recovery Tabletops Now Include the Agent
items.brief: Incident tabletops schedule the coding agent as a participant, because during a real incident it will be one. The templates cover the uncomfortable case: the agent's suggestion conflicts with the runbook, and half the room trusts it.

items.title: The Code Review Queue After AI: More Reviews, Less Reviewing
items.brief: AI-generated pull requests doubled queue length and halved average attention per review, which is the same problem wearing two hats. Teams that fixed it changed the contract: authors, human or not, ship smaller diffs or wait longer.

items.title: Prompt Debt Is Technical Debt: a Postmortem Taxonomy
items.brief: Prompt debt behaves like technical debt with worse telemetry: it accumulates invisibly, fails in production, and the fix is one line nobody wrote down. A taxonomy drawn from twenty postmortems, sorted by who had to discover the undocumented behavior.

items.title: When the Coding Agent Opens a PR: Ownership Without a Human Author
items.brief: When the agent opens the pull request, blame gets philosophically interesting and operationally simple: the human who merged it owns it. The argument is that the review trail, not authorship, is the accountability surface.

items.title: Retrieval Is an Org Chart Problem
items.brief: Retrieval quality problems are usually routing problems: the answer existed, but it lived in a repo, a wiki, and three heads, and the system indexed only the repo. Fixing retrieval meant fixing who owns which document — an org chart with a search bar.

items.title: The Quiet Rise of the Internal AI Platform Team
items.brief: The internal AI platform team — model access, evals, guardrails, cost accounting — arrived without a mandate and became the bottleneck nobody budgeted for. A look at how four companies scoped it before it scoped itself.

items.title: Evaluations That Survive Contact With a Real Backlog
items.brief: Evaluation suites that survive real backlogs share three properties: they run in CI, they fail loudly on regressions users would feel, and product owns the cases. Everything else is a demo that rots.

items.title: AI Meeting Notes Changed Who Owns the Record
items.brief: Automatic meeting notes settled an old argument by accident: whoever controls the summary controls the record, and now the model does. Teams are quietly writing policies for an archive no human transcribed.

items.title: Context Budgets: Why Your Agent Forgets the Roadmap
items.brief: Context budgets explain a whole class of agent misbehavior: the roadmap got truncated to make room for a stack trace, so the agent confidently shipped last quarter's plan. Budgeting context like memory — with priorities and eviction — fixes most of it.

items.title: Hiring When the Junior Tasks Are Gone
items.brief: The junior tasks are gone, so the ladder is being rebuilt in mid-air: apprenticeship now starts where verification starts, not where typing starts. Hiring managers describe what predicts success when the first job is reviewing, not writing.

items.title: A Field Audit of Our Own AI Usage Logs
items.brief: A month of internal usage logs, audited: what people actually paste in (less sensitive than policy feared), what they hide (more than anyone admitted), and where the real exposure turned out to be — telemetry, not prompts.

items.title: The Second-Order Effects of Auto-Generated Runbooks
items.brief: Auto-generated runbooks drift from the systems they describe at exactly the rate those systems change, which makes stale runbooks a leading indicator. The teams that benefit regenerate on deploy and stamp every page with the commit it describes.

items.title: Security Review for Agent Tool Calls: the Checklist That Stuck
items.brief: A security checklist for agent tool calls that survived a year in production: scope each tool, log every invocation with the prompt that triggered it, rate-limit by default. It exists because one agent, given a deployment tool, redeployed production on a guess.

items.title: The Economics of Self-Hosting in 2026
items.brief: Self-hosting economics in 2026: the hardware is cheap, the bandwidth is fine, and the real cost is the afternoon you lose to a certificate renewal at a family dinner. The spreadsheet behind the piece prices attention honestly, and the answer is still 'host the boring things.'

items.title: How Catalog Seed Companies Predict the Weather
items.brief: Seed catalogs are written a year ahead, which makes catalog copy a folk weather forecast: regional copy edits track drought years with uncanny fidelity. A small archival study with a great dataset.

items.title: The Lost Art of the Memorandum: How Writers Kept Thinking Before Notebooks
items.brief: Before note apps ate thinking, the memorandum did: one page, one claim, written to be filed and found. The form's constraints — brevity, single purpose, an assumption it would be retrieved — are exactly what modern tools lost.

items.title: A Beginner's Guide to Reading Handwritten Census Records
items.brief: Reading census handwriting is a learnable skill with about thirty recurring traps: doubled letters, enumerator shorthand, names spelled phonetically by ear. The guide teaches the traps as a system rather than a list.

items.title: Why Public Transit Maps Lie: a Cartographer's Confession
items.brief: Every transit map is a lie agreed upon: distances distorted, rivers bent, walking distances erased. What maps actually optimize for, and why the honest map turns out to be unusable.

items.title: The Quiet Comeback of the Mechanical Watch
items.brief: The mechanical watch returned as an object of maintenance rather than status: something you wind, service, and keep alive across decades. A week on a repair bench, following rescues.

items.title: What Fermentation Teaches About Patience and Failure
items.brief: Fermentation teaches the specific patience of watching a process you can neither rush nor reverse, with failure that is obvious only in hindsight. An essay that stays on the right side of metaphor.

items.title: The Anatomy of a Good Path
items.brief: Trail designers route a path by what the walker will tolerate: grade, sightlines, and the promise that the map matches the ground. The same geometry explains why some campus shortcuts survive paving and some do not.

items.title: How Luthiers Tune Wood
items.brief: Luthiers tune wood before building with it, tapping plates and listening for modes the finished guitar will carry. The craft sits at the exact edge of what can be measured and what must be heard.

items.title: The Archive of Forgotten Desktop Environments
items.brief: An archive of forgotten desktop environments is an archive of arguments about how people work: shells, spatial file managers, zooming interfaces, each lost for reasons that were never 'bad code.' The screenshots do the time travel.

items.title: Star Charts on Paper: the History of Celestial Atlases
items.brief: Celestial atlases solved a hard layout problem — mapping a sphere onto a page without lying about the sky — and their solutions track the history of print itself. A survey with plates worth the paper they lost.

items.title: A Walk Through the Last Public Phone Museum
items.brief: One of the last museums of public telephony, where every exhibit is the same object solving one problem across a century of hardware. The restored audio booths still take calls.

items.title: The Typography of Train Stations
items.brief: Station lettering had to work wet, dark, and at a glance, which is why it became the ancestor of the sans-serifs now on your screen. The story runs from railway signage plates to the family this page is set in.

items.title: Why We Still Build Cathedrals
items.brief: Cathedrals were built on timelines no individual could expect to see finished, by institutions optimizing for permanence over schedule. What a cathedral project looks like when the institution is a software project and the timeline is forty years.
